tableNotes.purpose: The plan document, and all four kinds of it: coach template, assigned client instance, self-coached personal plan, product-shipped system starter. `scope` discriminates and a table-level CHECK makes every incoherent owner combination unrepresentable, so the roadmap's is_template boolean is collapsed into it. Carries the scheduling RULE (cycle_days + starts_on), a trigger-bumped `revision` that logs snapshot, and source_plan_id/source_revision for clone provenance.
tableNotes.ownership: Coach: author_user_id = ? plus an EXISTS on an ACTIVE coach_clients link. Client: client_user_id = ? alone, with no status filter, so a client keeps their plan after being archived. trg_plan_link_client_ins/_upd prove the link actually joins that author to that client — the guard no CHECK can express.

tableNotes.purpose: A session slot in the cycle, addressed by (day_index, slot) — a position in the CYCLE, never a date. `slot` makes genuine two-a-days representable; is_rest makes a prescribed rest a real row so adherence does not count it as missed. day_index is bounded against the parent's cycle_days in both directions by trigger.
tableNotes.ownership: Through plan_id in one WHERE clause: AND plan_id = (SELECT ... the plan guard ...).

tableNotes.purpose: The superset/circuit container. EVERY exercise belongs to a block including a solo one (kind='single'), so ordering inside a day is total and no renderer needs an 'is this grouped' branch. A real table because a circuit repeats the BLOCK while a straight set repeats the EXERCISE, so rounds/rest/cap have nowhere else to live. day_id lives here and nowhere else, which is what prevents the block-move desync a critic found in a candidate.
tableNotes.ownership: plan_id, trigger-enforced to match the day's plan_id.

tableNotes.purpose: The prescription: exercise, sets, reps range OR time OR distance, load, %1RM, RPE, tempo, rest, load_mode. exercise_id is ON DELETE SET NULL beside a NOT NULL name snapshot — neither CASCADE (holes in live plans) nor RESTRICT (undeletable coach accounts, unfixable by any later migration).
tableNotes.ownership: plan_id, trigger-enforced to match the block's plan_id. trg_plan_exercise_visible_* additionally refuses any exercise that is not global or the plan author's own.

tableNotes.purpose: Optional per-set refinement — waves, top sets with backoffs, warm-up ramps, terminal AMRAPs. When absent, startWorkoutTx expands target_sets uniformly, so the branch lives in exactly one transaction and never in a renderer. Bounded against the parent's target_sets in both directions so the editor's '3 sets' and the player's 4 cannot disagree.
tableNotes.ownership: plan_id, trigger-enforced to match the exercise's plan_id.

tableNotes.purpose: The sparse diff against the scheduling rule: skip this Tuesday, move it to Wednesday. One row only when a human intervenes, so a plan running normally for a year costs nothing — this is what lets a rule-based calendar survive real life without materialising every session.
tableNotes.ownership: plan_id, trigger-enforced to match the day's plan_id.

tableNotes.purpose: ICS subscription credentials. A calendar client cannot send an HttpOnly cookie, so the feed URL carries a bearer secret — hashed at rest like invite_codes, shown in plaintext once, with a mandatory expires_at and an independent revoked_at so one leaked feed can die without breaking every other subscriber.
tableNotes.ownership: user_id = ? for management; the fetch path resolves token_hash and re-asserts the link is still active, and the archive transaction revokes coach-held feeds.

tableNotes.purpose: One training session, and a freestyle workout is this same row with plan_id/plan_day_id NULL. Snapshots plan_revision plus the plan and day names so history renders after the plan is rewritten or deleted; snapshots bodyweight_kg and the server-computed local_date so analytics never depend on a profile that changes. Holds the only stored aggregates in the schema.
tableNotes.ownership: Client: client_user_id = ?. Coach: coach_client_id = ? plus an EXISTS on an ACTIVE link. trg_log_plan_shape_ins/trg_log_plan_day_ins/trg_log_link_client_ins block attaching a log to a stranger's plan, day or link.

tableNotes.purpose: One exercise inside one session. Snapshots the display name ONCE per session (not per set) so history survives a rename, a soft delete, and the hard delete that follows a coach's account deletion. Carries origin (plan/added/substituted) so off-plan work and substitutions are first-class rather than a gap, plus a grouping snapshot as two scalars rather than an FK to a block that may be regrouped tomorrow.
tableNotes.ownership: client_user_id = ?, trigger-enforced against the parent log on INSERT and UPDATE. trg_log_exercise_visible_ins is the ACL that stops a client self-granting read access to a coach's private library.

tableNotes.purpose: The hot table. Rows are materialised as 'pending' at session start carrying their own frozen prescription, so a set check is a guarded UPDATE and the player needs nothing from the plan. effective_load_kg / volume_kg / e1rm_canonical_kg are STORED GENERATED, so no code path can put a client-supplied derived value here. write_uid is the per-attempt idempotency token; voided_at is the only permitted mutation after completion.
tableNotes.ownership: client_user_id = ? in the same WHERE as the idempotency guard — one table, no join. log_id/client_user_id/exercise_id/local_date are trigger-enforced against the parents so the denormalisation cannot become a cross-tenant write.

tableNotes.purpose: PR EVENTS, not current bests — there is deliberately no current-bests cache anywhere. 'My best' is one index descent; 'a badge was shown on 3 March and a coin was paid for it' is not derivable, so only that is stored, append-only with an invalidated_at tombstone. Three kinds: e1rm (primary), rep_max (bucketed 1-13), session_volume.
tableNotes.ownership: client_user_id = ?, and trg_pr_event_owner refuses at INSERT any event whose source set or log belongs to someone else.

tableNotes.purpose: The missing bridge that makes the avoid-list suggestion filter implementable at all: onboarding_limitations.body_area is joint-centric while exercises are tagged by muscle group, and nothing joined the two. WITHOUT ROWID junction, seeded by SLUG, with a loads/stabilises relation so a knee complaint does not remove every exercise a calf has ever stabilised.
tableNotes.ownership: Reference data. Admin-editable as a table rather than frozen as a CHECK, because the mapping is a clinical judgement that will be corrected without a migration.

decisions.question: Which file number?
decisions.answer: 010_plans_and_logs.sql, targeting user_version 10 — NOT 009 as the brief specified.
decisions.why: I listed the migrations directory: 009_language_roster.sql already exists and the DB is at user_version 9. worker.js:131 skips any file whose version <= current and reports success, so a second 009 would never run, migrate() would return {applied:[],version:9}, the port would bind, /readyz would pass, and every plan endpoint would 500 with 'no such table'. There is no error path for a duplicate number. Both reality critics flagged this as fatal against all three candidates.
decisions.rejected: Obeying the brief literally. Also rejected: leaving the runner unchanged — a duplicate migration number should crash at boot, which is a separate one-line fix in index.js I did not bundle into this migration.

decisions.question: How is 'a replayed set-check must not double-count' guaranteed?
decisions.answer: Four independent layers, all SQL-level: pending rows so a check is an UPDATE not an INSERT; a per-attempt write_uid in the UPDATE's own WHERE; trigger-maintained recompute-by-aggregate rollups; and two partial UNIQUE indexes on the PR event table.
decisions.why: Each layer alone has a hole. State-keyed idempotency (what every candidate used) cannot tell a replay from a correction, so an offline queue flushing a 100 kg typo and its 10 kg fix lands whichever arrived last and answers 200 either way. write_uid makes the key request IDENTITY, so a differing payload against a completed set changes zero rows and gets a 409.
decisions.rejected: A generic idempotency_keys table (needs a TTL sweeper, stored response bodies, and a definition of 'the same request' — every write here already has a natural key). A monotonic client sequence counter (silently discards real writes forever when a client reinstalls and restarts at 1, and reports the loss as success).

decisions.question: Mutable plans or immutable versioned plans?
decisions.answer: Plans stay mutable documents; the LOG snapshots the prescription onto every set row at session start, plus plan_revision and the plan/day/exercise names.
decisions.why: The integrity requirement is not that the plan be immutable, it is that 'did the client hit the prescription?' stays answerable forever. Snapshotting achieves that even after the plan is rewritten the next morning or deleted next month, and it survives plan_id going NULL. It is the order-line price-snapshot pattern.
decisions.rejected: Copy-on-write plan versions (needs a version-cleanup policy, and still does not survive account deletion). A live join to workout_plan_exercises at render time (cheapest storage, but it makes history a view of mutable data and a plan delete a history delete).

decisions.question: Can a completed set be edited?
decisions.answer: No. trg_log_set_frozen makes measurements immutable at trigger level; the only mutation is a void, which leaves a tombstone plus reason and is itself terminal.
decisions.why: Three of six critic passes found the same fatal bug in candidates that allowed edits: an endpoint that is simultaneously the replay path and the correction path, leaving a personal record no surviving set supports, and — because the server resolves target_percent_1rm from that record — prescribing 85% of a lift that never happened. Immutability makes the whole class unrepresentable.
decisions.rejected: Allowing in-place correction while the log is still in_progress. Softer UX, but a gold badge has already been shown by then and once coins exist money has already moved. This is real friction and is listed as an open question.

decisions.question: How is the 1RM stored so a future formula change does not break records?
decisions.answer: e1rm_canonical_kg is a STORED GENERATED column: Epley over effective load, pinned forever, used by every comparison and every index. The 1RM the product DISPLAYS is computed in JS at read time and stored nowhere.
decisions.why: A candidate stored 'the current formula' with a tag and indexed it. Switching Epley to Brzycki then compares two different quantities under one ORDER BY: every user silently stops earning records until they out-lift the ~3% gap, high-rep lifters get a wave of unearned badges, and no repair exists short of voiding real training. Splitting comparison from display makes a formula change a rendering change.
decisions.rejected: A plain app-written column with an e1rm_formula tag (the index has no formula term, so the comparison still mixes scales; and the arithmetic CHECK was conditioned on the tag, so any non-Epley row was written unverified). Computing 1RM only on read (correct, but unindexable, so PR detection becomes a full scan).

decisions.question: How does a client read a coach's private exercise without a self-service ACL?
decisions.answer: Access is DERIVED from prescription through a LIVE coach_clients link, and trg_log_exercise_visible_ins refuses any log row referencing an exercise the client could not already read.
decisions.why: exercises/routes.js:26 makes a coach's private exercise invisible to their own client, so the plan 404s. But two candidates fixed it by granting read on 'anything I have personally performed' — and the client writes the row that constitutes proof, so an ordinary user could POST one freestyle log row per exercise_id 1..1652 and dump every coach's private library, every pending_review submission and every rejection_reason.
decisions.rejected: A workout_exercise_grants capability table (nothing revoked it when the plan item was removed, and its granted_by was nullable so the archive DELETE missed rows). Extending VISIBLE globally with an EXISTS over coach_clients (hands the client the coach's entire library, drafts included).

decisions.question: Materialised calendar or scheduling rule?
decisions.answer: A rule — (starts_on, cycle_days, day_index) — diffed against a sparse workout_plan_day_exceptions table.
decisions.why: A year of a plan running normally costs zero rows, 'push Thursday to Friday' is one INSERT, and there is no horizon top-up job to forget. cycle_days<=56 plus trg_plan_day_in_cycle_* bound the occurrence count, so generation cannot be driven unbounded by a client number.
decisions.rejected: One row per scheduled session (Design 1). It makes the Home card a point lookup, but it needs a repair path for every plan edit after assignment — deleting a day silently deletes future sessions with no audit row — and its expansion is an unbounded write inside one IMMEDIATE transaction, i.e. a self-serve write-lock DoS.

decisions.question: Are session rollups stored, and how are they kept honest?
decisions.answer: Stored, maintained by trg_log_rollup_recompute_* on every set write, and guarded by trg_log_rollup_truthful which refuses any value that is not the true aggregate.
decisions.why: My own attack suite caught this: with the rollups merely absent from the freeze trigger, a PATCH set total_volume_kg to 999999 on a CLOSED session and it was accepted. The coach dashboard reads that column instead of re-aggregating. The truthfulness trigger is stronger than freezing because it also holds while the session is live, and it removes the 'code discipline' weakness every candidate admitted to.
decisions.rejected: Leaving the recompute to the application (three transactions today, a fourth next year written by someone who did not read the file). Storing nothing (the coach dashboard would then aggregate across every client's every set per page load).

decisions.question: Unique or non-unique ordering indexes?
decisions.answer: Non-unique on `position` with `id` as tie-break; UNIQUE only on semantic coordinates (day_index+slot, set_index).
decisions.why: SQLite checks UNIQUE per statement, not deferred to commit, so a drag-reorder rewriting positions 0..n-1 in one transaction collides part-way and aborts a perfectly legal reorder. A duplicate position is cosmetically harmless; an aborted reorder is a bug report.
decisions.rejected: UNIQUE(day_id, position) with a two-pass 'park everything at +1000000' shuffle (Design 1). It works, but it is machinery every future contributor must rediscover, and it leaves `position` with no upper bound purely to host the parking range.

decisions.question: How is bodyweight training represented?
decisions.answer: A load_mode enum (external/bodyweight/weighted_bodyweight/assisted) plus a bodyweight_kg snapshot on the set row, feeding a generated effective_load_kg.
decisions.why: Every candidate defined volume as weight_kg*reps, so a calisthenics client reports 0 kg forever, an empty progress graph and no possible weight or 1RM record — and one candidate snapshotted bodyweight onto the log while giving it no consumer. bodyweight_kg is denormalised onto the set because a generated column may not contain a subquery.
decisions.rejected: Deriving bodyweight volume at read time (unindexable, and the PR path needs it inside the write transaction). Ignoring assisted work (an assisted pull-up would report its counterweight as the lift).

decisions.question: Civil dates as INTEGER or TEXT?
decisions.why: date() round-tripping is an exact validator — it rejects 2026-08-33, 2026-13-01, 2026-02-30 (normalised to 03-02, so equality fails) and unpadded 2026-8-5. TEXT also makes date(local_date,'+7 days') correct SQL. Design 1's packed YYYYMMDD integer accepts 20260833 and makes scheduled_on+7 a silent corruption its own author flagged.
decisions.rejected: YYYYMMDD INTEGER (keeps the 'timestamps are INTEGER' rule superficially but breaks date arithmetic and admits impossible dates). Epoch-of-local-midnight (only correct for one timezone, and nothing in the type says which).

indexRationale: workout_plans_author_idx (author_user_id, scope, archived_at) — the coach's library screen and the template picker: my templates, live ones first.
workout_plans_client_idx (client_user_id, status, archived_at) — the client's plan list and the Home 'today' card, which is the single most-loaded query in the product.
workout_plans_link_idx (coach_client_id, status) — the coach's client-detail tab, joined live through the link so archiving ends access on the very next read.
workout_plans_source_idx (source_plan_id) WHERE NOT NULL — 'which clients are on this template', the query that makes a bulk re-clone previewable.
workout_plans_system_idx (scope, goal, experience) WHERE scope='system' — starter-library browse filtered by the onboarding answers.

workout_plan_days_slot_unique (plan_id, day_index, slot) UNIQUE — semantic coordinate; without it 'what am I doing on Tuesday' is nondeterministic and copy-week run twice produces two week-2s. Also the covering index the adherence query's outer side uses (verified by EXPLAIN).

workout_plan_blocks_day_idx (day_id, position, id) — renders a day in order; deliberately NOT unique, because SQLite checks UNIQUE per statement and a drag-reorder rewriting 0..n-1 would abort mid-way. `id` keeps the order total when two positions collide.

workout_plan_exercises_exercise_idx (exercise_id) WHERE NOT NULL — serves both 'which plans use this exercise' (the pre-delete warning for a coach editing their library) and the client-visibility EXISTS. Verified: the visibility EXISTS plans as SEARCH px USING INDEX workout_plan_exercises_exercise_idx.

workout_logs_client_idx (client_user_id, local_date DESC, id DESC) — the history feed, streaks and calendar; local_date leads because the user's DAY is what all three group by, and `id` makes the pagination cursor total.

workout_logs_adherence_idx (plan_day_id, occurrence_date) WHERE plan_day_id IS NOT NULL — deliberately plain and status-free. The adherence LEFT JOIN's ON clause implies plan_day_id IS NOT NULL and nothing else, and SQLite only uses a partial index when the query provably implies its predicate, so the status-qualified unique index cannot serve it. Without this index the planner full-scans the largest table once per outer row. Verified: SEARCH l USING COVERING INDEX workout_logs_adherence_idx.

workout_logs_one_live_unique (client_user_id) WHERE status='in_progress' UNIQUE — one live session per client, so two phones cannot start two set grids that each later claim the same record. Scoped to in_progress, not <>abandoned, so a completed log does not permanently block a second evening session.

workout_logs_occurrence_unique (client_user_id, plan_day_id, occurrence_date) WHERE plan_day_id IS NOT NULL AND status='in_progress' UNIQUE — a double-tapped Start collides here instead of producing twins.
workout_log_sets_slot_unique (log_exercise_id, set_index) UNIQUE — the player's grid and the natural key that makes 'previous performance for set 3' unambiguous.
workout_log_sets_log_idx (log_id, voided_at, set_kind) — the rollup recompute the three trigger bodies run, and the 'n of m sets done' chip.

workout_log_sets_progress_idx (client_user_id, exercise_id, local_date DESC, id DESC, weight_kg, reps, effective_load_kg, volume_kg, e1rm_canonical_kg) WHERE voided_at IS NULL AND completed_at IS NOT NULL AND set_kind<>'warmup' — COVERING: the months-long progress graph and the player's PREVIOUS column read entirely from the index. Partial, so voided sets and warm-ups are not in the B-tree at all and a query that forgets a term cannot include them. Verified: SEARCH ... USING INDEX workout_log_sets_progress_idx, no TEMP B-TREE.
workout_log_sets_repmax_idx (client_user_id, exercise_id, reps, effective_load_kg DESC) WHERE ... — 'heaviest ever at exactly 5 reps' is one seek to the head of the DESC run. Verified.

workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx (client_user_id, exercise_id, e1rm_canonical_kg DESC) WHERE ... AND e1rm_canonical_kg IS NOT NULL — the record seek. The predicate is the NULL test rather than a reps range on purpose: with a reps range the query must repeat it and the planner then prefers repmax_idx plus a TEMP B-TREE sort. Verified clean.

workout_log_sets_exercise_idx (exercise_id, client_user_id) WHERE NOT NULL — non-partial deliberately, because the covering progress index cannot serve a query that does not repeat its three-term predicate and SQLite will not infer the implication. Serves the moderation queue's 'has anyone logged this'.
workout_pr_events_source_unique (source_set_id, kind, rep_bucket) WHERE source_set_id IS NOT NULL AND invalidated_at IS NULL UNIQUE — the replay backstop, and therefore the double-award backstop.

workout_pr_events_day_unique (client_user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket, local_date) WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL UNIQUE — the ON CONFLICT target that collapses an ascending ramp to one event per day and makes the outcome order-insensitive.
workout_pr_events_feed_idx (client_user_id, achieved_at DESC) WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL — the 'recent PRs' strip on the profile and the coach's client feed.
body_area_muscle_map_muscle_idx (muscle_group_id, relation) — the reverse direction: given an exercise's muscle tags, which limitations does it trip?
idempotencyDesign:
"FOUR INDEPENDENT SQL-LEVEL LAYERS. All of it runs inside ONE named worker transaction (recordSetTx) using tx.immediate(), which takes the single write lock on the first statement — so there is no window between a read and its write, and the same code under a DEFERRED transaction would be a TOCTOU. Every branch that can produce an error result runs strictly BEFORE the first write, per ADR-0005's commit-on-return law.

LAYER 0 — THERE IS NO INSERT TO DUPLICATE. startWorkoutTx materialises the whole grid as 'pending' rows, so checking a set is an UPDATE. The entire double-tap duplicate-row class is gone before any dedupe logic runs.

LAYER 1 — THE GUARD IS THE UPDATE, and the key is REQUEST IDENTITY, not row state:

  UPDATE workout_log_sets
     SET completed_at = COALESCE(completed_at, unixepoch()),
         weight_kg = :w, entry_unit = :u, entry_value = :ev, reps = :r,
         seconds = :s, distance_m = :d, rpe = :rpe, rest_taken_seconds = :rest,
         write_uid = :uid
   WHERE id = :id AND client_user_id = :me AND voided_at IS NULL
     AND (completed_at IS NULL OR write_uid = :uid);

Three outcomes, all decided by the database:
  * fresh check   -> changes = 1. Proceed to the PR upsert.
  * exact replay  -> the same :uid matches, the row is rewritten with identical values, still ONE row. Everything downstream is idempotent, so the net effect is nil. Reported 200 {applied:false, replayed:true}, following onboarding/routes.js:243 — a double-tapped submit is the client's most ordinary mistake and must not read as a failure.
  * DIFFERENT payload against a completed set -> matches nothing, changes = 0. The route re-reads the row (no write happened, so returning an error here is ADR-0005-safe) and answers 409 with the stored values, so the client offers void-and-relog.
That third case is the one every candidate design got wrong: keying on completed_at alone makes 'the same request twice' and 'a corrected value' indistinguishable, so an offline queue flushing a 100 kg typo and its 10 kg correction persists whichever the network delivered last and answers 200 either way — the user's screen and their history disagree permanently, and the freeze trigger then makes it uncorrectable.

Ownership is in the same WHERE: `client_user_id = :me` on a trigger-enforced denormalised column. changes = 0 with no matching row is a 404, never a 403.

LAYER 2 — DERIVED NUMBERS CANNOT BE INFLATED, BY CONSTRUCTION. effective_load_kg, volume_kg and e1rm_canonical_kg are STORED GENERATED columns: no INSERT or UPDATE surface exists, so no code path — forged through a proxy or refactored in a hurry — can put a client-supplied volume or 1RM into the database. Re-running the same write recomputes the same value.

LAYER 3 — ROLLUPS ARE RECOMPUTED, NEVER INCREMENTED, AND MAY NOT LIE. trg_log_rollup_recompute_ins/_upd/_del fire on every set write and rewrite the parent log's five totals as `SET x = (SELECT SUM(...))` over ~25 rows behind workout_log_sets_log_idx. `SET x = (SELECT SUM(...))` is idempotent by construction; `SET x = x + ?` is not, and an increment is exactly what a replay double-counts. Separately trg_log_rollup_truthful REFUSES any UPDATE that names a rollup column and sets it to something other than the true aggregate — so a route that spreads req.body cannot forge a tonnage even on a live session. (My attack suite caught this: before that trigger existed, `UPDATE workout_logs SET total_volume_kg=999999` on a CLOSED session was accepted.)

LAYER 4 — THE RECORD IS A GUARDED UPSERT WITH TWO UNIQUE BACKSTOPS. Values are computed in the worker from the row's own generated columns, never from anything the client sent:

  INSERT INTO workout_pr_events
    (client_user_id, exercise_id, exercise_name_snapshot, source_set_id, log_id,
     kind, rep_bucket, value, previous_value, local_date)
  VALUES (:me, :ex, :nm, :setId, :logId, :kind, :bucket, :val, :prev, :date)
  ON CONFLICT (client_user_id, exercise_id, kind, rep_bucket, local_date)
    WHERE invalidated_at IS NULL
  DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value, source_set_id = excluded.source_set_id,
                log_id = excluded.log_id, achieved_at = unixepoch()
   WHERE excluded.value > workout_pr_events.value + 0.005;

The comparison lives INSIDE the UPDATE — no preceding SELECT, no race. changes = 1 means and can only mean a genuinely better value; a replay produces excluded.value = the stored value, the guard is false, changes = 0, no badge. The +0.005 epsilon is deliberate: lb->kg conversion means the same physical lift does not produce bit-identical floats, and a bare `>` mints a phantom record for repeating 225 lb after a client-side rounding change.

  * workout_pr_events_source_unique (source_set_id, kind, rep_bucket) WHERE source_set_id IS NOT NULL AND invalidated_at IS NULL — at most one live event per set per kind. Even if every guard above were defeated, a second event for the same set cannot exist. Because a coin will be granted against a workout_pr_events ROW, the same index that stops a double record stops a double award: one constraint, both requirements, and no reward column invented here.
  * workout_pr_events_day_unique — the ON CONFLICT target above. It is NOT about replays: a lifter ramping 90/95/100/102.5/105 kg past their old best mints FIVE events under a naive per-set append, because each set legitimately beats the one before. Five badges, later five coins, for one session. With this index the write only ever moves the day's event UP, so the final state is 'the best of that day' regardless of the order an offline queue delivered in — which also makes the record count deterministic rather than a function of the client's network. Verified: 90/95/100/102.5/105 in any order yields exactly one row at the max.
  * rep_bucket is NOT NULL with a 0 sentinel rather than nullable, because SQLite treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index — a nullable rep_bucket would let two 'e1rm' rows coexist for one set and the backstop would silently not exist while appearing to.

CORRECTIONS AND VOIDS. A completed set is immutable (trg_log_set_frozen); the only mutation is voidSetTx, which sets voided_at + voided_reason, stamps invalidated_at on the events whose source_set_id it was, and lets the rollup triggers recompute — all in one transaction. Voiding is terminal (trg_log_set_void_terminal), so a set cannot be resurrected into the analytics indexes while its record still carries a tombstone. Because the day-unique index is partial on invalidated_at IS NULL, invalidating frees the day slot and a genuine later record on the same day can still be recorded.

OTHER REPLAY SURFACES CLOSED THE SAME WAY: workout_logs_one_live_unique (one live session per client) and workout_logs_occurrence_unique (one live session per prescribed occurrence) make a double-tapped Start collide at the database. startWorkoutTx must still read for an existing live log before its first write and return it as 200 {resumed:true}, because lib/http.js has no typed mapping for SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE and would render it as a 500 to someone standing in a gym — the index is the backstop, not the user experience. A replayed finish is `UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND client_user_id=? AND status='in_progress'`; changes = 0 means already finished, and every rollup is skipped.

VERIFIED, not asserted: the migration was executed against SQLite 3.53.2 through better-sqlite3-multiple-ciphers on a stand-in of the live schema, and a 76-assertion suite exercised first write, exact replay, differing-payload replay, the ascending ramp, out-of-order delivery, void, un-void, replayed finish and rollup forgery. All green."
ownershipMatrix: workout_plans (COACH write/read of an instance or template): WHERE id = ? AND author_user_id = ? AND archived_at IS NULL AND (coach_client_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = workout_plans.coach_client_id AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active'))  -- author alone is NOT sufficient: it would let an archived coach keep editing a plan they still own. The EXISTS is what makes archiving take effect on the very next request with the same unexpired token.

workout_plans (CLIENT read): WHERE client_user_id = ? AND archived_at IS NULL AND status <> 'draft'  -- single-table, no join, and deliberately NO link-status filter: a client keeps their plan and history after a coach archives them. They own their training; the coach owned only the relationship.

workout_plan_days / _blocks / _exercises / _set_targets / _day_exceptions (COACH write): WHERE id = ? AND plan_id = (SELECT p.id FROM workout_plans p WHERE p.id = ? AND p.author_user_id = ? AND p.archived_at IS NULL AND (p.coach_client_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = p.coach_client_id AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active')))  -- this is why plan_id is denormalised onto every node of the authoring tree: one WHERE clause, no application-side walk, changes = 0 -> 404. INSERTs use the same predicate as INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE EXISTS, and the parent-coherence triggers make the denormalised plan_id unforgeable.

workout_plan_days / _blocks / _exercises / _set_targets (CLIENT read): WHERE plan_id IN (SELECT id FROM workout_plans WHERE client_user_id = ? AND archived_at IS NULL AND status <> 'draft')  -- one indexed subquery on workout_plans_client_idx.

workout_calendar_feeds (OWNER): WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?. (FEED FETCH, unauthenticated): WHERE token_hash = ? AND revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > unixepoch() AND (coach_client_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = workout_calendar_feeds.coach_client_id AND cc.status = 'active'))  -- the token authenticates, the link authorises, and the archive transaction additionally revokes.
workout_logs (CLIENT, read and write): WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ?  -- single-table. The set-check path never climbs a level to find an owner.

workout_logs (COACH read): WHERE coach_client_id = ? AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM coach_clients cc WHERE cc.id = ? AND cc.coach_id = ? AND cc.status = 'active')  -- keyed on the LINK id from the URL (/clients/:linkId/logs), never the client's user id, exactly as onboarding/routes.js:255-265. A coach never WRITES a client's log; there is no route for it.

workout_log_exercises (CLIENT): WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ?  -- the denormalised owner is enforced against the parent log on INSERT by trg_log_exercise_parent_ins and on UPDATE by trg_log_exercise_parent_upd, so it cannot be used to forge a claim. (COACH read): WHERE log_id IN (SELECT l.id FROM workout_logs l WHERE l.coach_client_id = ? AND EXISTS (...active link...)).

workout_log_sets (CLIENT, and this is the hottest write in the product): WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ? AND voided_at IS NULL AND (completed_at IS NULL OR write_uid = ?)  -- ownership and idempotency in the same WHERE, one table, no join. trg_log_set_parent_ins/_upd keep log_id, client_user_id, exercise_id and local_date matching the parents, so the denormalisation cannot be turned into a cross-tenant write. (COACH read): via the log's link predicate above.

workout_pr_events (CLIENT): WHERE id = ? AND client_user_id = ?; list reads add AND invalidated_at IS NULL. trg_pr_event_owner refuses at INSERT any event whose source_set_id or log_id belongs to a different client, so a record cannot be minted against a stranger's set — cosmetic today, a credit transfer once coins exist. (COACH read): WHERE client_user_id = (SELECT client_id FROM coach_clients WHERE id = ? AND coach_id = ? AND status = 'active')  -- a NULL subquery matches nothing, so an archived link yields an empty result rather than an error, and the miss is indistinguishable from a denial.

body_area_muscle_map: reference data, no ownership. Read by everyone, written only by an admin route behind requireRole (which returns 403, the documented exception to 404-not-403 — a role gate leaks nothing about which rows exist).

onboarding_profiles.timezone (the ALTERed column): WHERE user_id = ? for the owner; the coach reads it only through the existing link-scoped onboarding predicate. It is a HINT — workout_logs.local_date is computed server-side from it and never taken from a request.
openQuestions: Void-only correction is real UX friction. Tapping the wrong row is common, and the answer here is a strikethrough tombstone with a reason. Does the player HIDE voided rows (losing the transparency the immutability buys) or SHOW them (looking broken to the user)? I would not soften the trigger, but the product owner should decide the rendering — and whether a void within, say, 60 seconds of the check is presented as a plain 'undo' instead.

rep_max records are noisy for beginners: a novice who has never done a set of 7 gets a badge the first time they do one, at any weight. That devalues the badge in month one. The fix (only fire rep_max when the weight also exceeds the best at every higher rep count) is a query change, not a schema change — but someone should decide whether beginners get the noisy version deliberately, for motivation.

The body_area to muscle_group map is a blunt heuristic. 'Avoid knee' removes leg extensions (right), leg press (arguable) and hip thrusts (wrong), and it MISSES exercises that load a joint without training its muscles (a plank stresses wrists). Proper modelling needs per-exercise joint-action tags across 1652 rows, which neither wger nor free-exercise-db provides. Ship the heuristic with a coach override, or wait for the dataset work?

There is no propagation path from a template to its clones. A coach running 40 clients on one programme who spots a bad rep range must re-clone 40 plans, losing per-client tweaks. source_plan_id makes a bulk re-clone previewable but I did not design the diff/merge that would make it safe. Is 'edit it 40 times' acceptable for v1, or does this need a propagation feature before launch?

One live session per client is enforced by a partial unique index. It kills the two-phones bug, but a client who forgets to tap Finish yesterday cannot start today's workout until something abandons the stale one. The stale-session sweeper (finish sessions with >=1 completed set and no activity for N hours, abandon those with none) is not schema — what should N be, and should the client be shown a 'resume or discard' prompt or handled silently?

ICS feed tokens expire (expires_at is NOT NULL) but the schema does not pick the lifetime. 90 days means users re-subscribe quarterly; 1 year means a leaked URL lives a year. This is a security-vs-annoyance call for the owner, not for me.

workout_plan_set_targets doubles the authoring surface (another CRUD, another reorder, another ownership predicate) to support ramps, waves and warm-up ladders the roadmap never explicitly asked for. It earns its place only if this is a real coaching tool rather than a template filler. Cutting it costs one branch in startWorkoutTx and nothing else in the schema.

missing: PR DETECTION FOR TIME- AND DISTANCE-BASED WORK IS UNREPRESENTABLE. The roadmap makes time-based prescriptions first-class in authoring (workout_plan_exercises.target_metric IN ('reps','time','distance'), target_seconds, target_distance_m) and then asks for 'PR detection with a badge'. But workout_pr_events.kind is CHECK (kind IN ('e1rm','rep_max','session_volume')) -- all three are load/rep measures. EXECUTED: inserting a 'time_max' record for a 90-second plank fails with `CHECK constraint failed: kind IN ('e1rm', 'rep_max', 'session_volume')`. A calisthenics, isometric or conditioning client can never earn a badge, and openQuestions never mentions it. Widening a CHECK later needs the 12-step table rebuild, which the file's own header says is unavailable inside a migration transaction -- so this is close to a one-way door.

SESSION_VOLUME PRs ARE UNSTORABLE FOR ANY ZERO-TONNAGE SESSION. `value REAL NOT NULL CHECK (value > 0)`. EXECUTED on a plank-only session: volume_kg is NULL (the generated column requires `reps IS NOT NULL AND reps > 0`), so total_volume_kg = 0, and the session_volume insert fails with `CHECK constraint failed: value > 0`. tableNotes says session_volume is 'written by the completion transaction' -- so finishWorkoutTx needs a branch nobody specified, and without it finishing a mobility/cardio session raises a CHECK that lib/http.js renders as a 500. Same failure shape as the attack-phase 'bodyweight set aborts the transaction' finding, relocated from the set path to the finish path.

'COPY WEEK' DOES NOT WORK ON THE DEFAULT PLAN SHAPE. EXECUTED against the stock cycle_days=7 client plan: `INSERT INTO workout_plan_days (plan_id, day_index, name) VALUES (200, 7, 'Push wk2')` aborts with `workout_plan_days.day_index must be inside the plan cycle` (trg_plan_day_in_cycle_ins). The coach must first `UPDATE workout_plans SET cycle_days = 14`, which is not a copy -- it re-dates every future occurrence of every existing day (a Monday session becomes fortnightly) and silently breaks the (plan_day_id, occurrence_date) adherence join for sessions already logged. The roadmap lists 'copy day / copy week' as one feature; copy-day works, copy-week is not expressible without changing the meaning of the plan. Neither decisions nor openQuestions addresses this.

ICS EXPORT CANNOT EMIT A TIME OF DAY. EXECUTED: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pragma_table_info('workout_plan_days') WHERE name LIKE '%time%'` returns 0. workout_plan_days has name, notes, is_rest, est_minutes -- no preferred_time, no start_time. workout_calendar_feeds carries no timezone either, and workout_plans has none. So every VEVENT is an all-day blob: the feed can say 'Leg day, Tuesday' and never 'Leg day, 18:00'. For the one roadmap feature whose entire point is landing in the user's calendar next to their other appointments, that is a material shortfall, and the design never states it as a deliberate scope cut.

PER-EXERCISE PROGRESS GRAPHS EXIST ONLY FOR LOADED WORK. workout_log_sets_progress_idx carries (client_user_id, exercise_id, local_date DESC, id DESC, weight_kg, reps, effective_load_kg, volume_kg, e1rm_canonical_kg) -- `seconds` and `distance_m` are absent. A plank-duration or 5k-time chart therefore falls off the index into a table lookup per row, and has no record series to plot a PR marker against (see the kind CHECK above). The indexRationale calls this index 'COVERING' for 'the months-long progress graph'; it is covering for barbell work only.

THE CLIENT-SIDE READ PATH FOR A PRESCRIBED PRIVATE EXERCISE IS NEVER WRITTEN. decisions says access 'is DERIVED from prescription through a LIVE coach_clients link', and trg_log_exercise_visible_ins encodes that predicate -- but only for WRITES to workout_log_exercises. exercises/routes.js:26's VISIBLE constant is untouched and `exercises` appears nowhere in the ownershipMatrix (11 rows, none for exercises). So the guided player can materialise a set for 'Coach Secret Lift' and render its name from the snapshot, while GET /exercises/101 still 404s for the client who is standing in the gym trying to read the instructions, the media and the muscle map. The roadmap's guided player and the 'plan suggestions' filter both need that read. The trigger contains the predicate; nothing promotes it to the read layer.

'PLAN SUGGESTIONS' HAS NOTHING TO SUGGEST. The FILTER is now buildable -- body_area_muscle_map seeds cleanly (EXECUTED: 44 rows, every one of the 20 slugs resolves against the 003 muscle_groups seed) and equipment already joins via onboarding_equipment -> exercise_equipment_map. But the only owner-less suggestible plan is scope='system', and the file's header explicitly ships that discriminator with zero content and defers workout_plan_translations to 'when the library ships'. So T2.5.4 is unblocked for exercise-level filtering and still blocked for plan-level suggestion. Worth stating openly rather than leaving the roadmap line looking satisfied.

AN ACTIVE CLIENT PLAN CAN HAVE starts_on NULL, AND THEN THE HOME 'TODAY' CARD IS SILENTLY EMPTY FOREVER. EXECUTED: `INSERT INTO workout_plans (scope='client', status='active', starts_on=NULL, ...)` is accepted. The whole calendar is (starts_on + k*cycle_days + day_index); with starts_on NULL the generator emits zero occurrences, the client sees a plan in their list and nothing on their home screen, and no constraint, trigger or index catches it. The obvious guard -- CHECK (status <> 'active' OR starts_on IS NOT NULL) -- is absent, and the design elsewhere is meticulous about exactly this class of table CHECK.
unaddressedFlaws: THE CLONE-SOURCE IDOR (attack: 'Coach->coach IDOR via source_plan_id') IS NEITHER FIXED NOR DISMISSED. workout_plans.source_plan_id is `INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plans(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` -- a bare, client-supplied, cross-tenant foreign key. EXECUTED: coach 4 inserted `INSERT INTO workout_plans (scope='template', author_user_id=4, source_plan_id=210, source_revision=1, ...)` where 210 is coach 1's private flagship template. Accepted, 1 row, no CHECK, no trigger. Every OTHER client-supplied cross-tenant FK in this file got a BEFORE INSERT trigger -- coach_client_id (trg_plan_link_client_ins), plan_id/plan_day_id (trg_log_plan_shape_ins/trg_log_plan_day_ins), exercise_id (trg_plan_exercise_visible_ins), log_id/client_user_id (trg_log_set_parent_ins), source_set_id (trg_pr_event_owner). source_plan_id is the single one left bare, and the ownershipMatrix's two workout_plans rows cover 'COACH write/read of an instance or template' and 'CLIENT read' -- neither is the clone SOURCE predicate, which is a read of someone else's row. The clone transaction reads the source's days, blocks, exercises, set targets and per-item notes and writes copies the attacker owns; workout_plans_source_idx then makes the theft self-documenting. decisions never mentions it; openQuestions mentions source_plan_id only for re-clone propagation. Given the design's own thesis -- 'this is the one guard that cannot live in a WHERE clause, which is exactly why it must be a trigger' -- this is the flaw the schema most clearly still owes.

THE DATA-LOSS HALF OF THE 'ON DELETE SET NULL STRANDS HISTORY' ATTACK IS UNADDRESSED. The design correctly swapped RESTRICT for SET NULL to un-brick account deletion, but never answered the second half the attack raised. exercises.owner_id is ON DELETE CASCADE from users (003), and workout_log_exercises.exercise_id, workout_log_sets.exercise_id and workout_pr_events.exercise_id are all ON DELETE SET NULL. So deleting one coach account nulls the join key on every one of their clients' historical sets: those rows drop out of workout_log_sets_progress_idx, workout_log_sets_repmax_idx, workout_log_sets_e1rm_idx and workout_log_sets_exercise_idx (all `WHERE exercise_id IS NOT NULL` or keyed on it), the progress graph goes blank, 'PREVIOUS performance' stops resolving, and because SQLite treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index, workout_pr_events_day_unique silently stops constraining those rows. The attack proposed a stable exercise_key; the design adopted neither that nor any alternative, and tableNotes still claims the snapshot means history 'renders forever' -- it renders, but it is no longer queryable as a series.

THE OFFLINE-QUEUE BATCH CONTRACT WAS DROPPED RATHER THAN FIXED. The attack found syncOfflineQueue structurally unimplementable (one IMMEDIATE tx + per-op results + throw-on-bad-op is any two of three under ADR-0005). The final design's response is to not have a batch endpoint at all -- yet idempotencyDesign leans on the offline queue four separate times ('an offline queue flushing a 100 kg typo and its 10 kg fix', 'regardless of the order an offline queue delivered in', 'a function of the client's network'). The per-set write is genuinely safe now. What is undefined is what happens when 24 queued ops flush: nothing specifies ordering, nothing specifies whether one 409 aborts the flush, and workout_logs_one_live_unique will raise SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE -- which lib/http.js has no typed mapping for -- if a queued 'start' op replays after a finish. The design acknowledges that gap for startWorkoutTx only, in a comment, as a route obligation.
sqlErrors: FATAL, VERIFIED: trg_log_set_server_columns re-opens the exact FK-action trap the file congratulates itself on closing, one table over. The trigger body lists `OR NEW.plan_set_target_id IS NOT OLD.plan_set_target_id` with NO transition-to-NULL carve-out -- while the very next-but-one clause, for exercise_id, correctly reads `OR (NEW.exercise_id IS NOT OLD.exercise_id AND NEW.exercise_id IS NOT NULL)`. The column is declared `plan_set_target_id INTEGER REFERENCES workout_plan_set_targets(id) ON DELETE SET NULL`, and an FK action IS an UPDATE as far as triggers are concerned -- which is precisely what the file's own comment on trg_workout_logs_frozen says: 'THE `IS NOT NULL` HALF OF EACH FK CLAUSE IS NOT DECORATION... it was only found by executing the migration and then running `DELETE FROM users`'. It was found for workout_logs and missed for workout_log_sets. EXECUTED, all four abort with `workout_log_sets: the prescription snapshot and load context are server-owned` once one client has trained one set materialised from a workout_plan_set_targets row: (1) DELETE FROM workout_plan_exercises WHERE id=500 -- a coach removing an exercise from a day, i.e. the plan editor's most ordinary operation; (2) DELETE FROM workout_plans WHERE id=200; (3) DELETE FROM coach_clients WHERE id=10 (workout_plans.coach_client_id is ON DELETE CASCADE, so it reaches the same SET NULL); (4) DELETE FROM users WHERE id=1 -- the coach's GDPR erasure, returning a generic 500. Control case: with plan_set_target_id NULL on the set, the identical plan delete succeeds (changes=1). Fix is one clause: `OR (NEW.plan_set_target_id IS NOT OLD.plan_set_target_id AND NEW.plan_set_target_id IS NOT NULL)`.

trg_log_set_void_terminal DOES NOT ENFORCE TERMINALITY -- it enforces timestamp inequality. `WHEN OLD.voided_at IS NOT NULL AND NEW.voided_at IS NOT OLD.voided_at`. EXECUTED: re-voiding an already-voided set inside the same wall-clock second (`SET voided_at = unixepoch(), voided_reason = 'y'`) yields NEW.voided_at = OLD.voided_at, the WHEN is false, and the UPDATE succeeds -- changes=1, voided_reason silently rewritten. One second later the identical statement aborts. So the guarantee the tableNotes state ('a void is terminal') holds or does not hold depending on clock granularity, which makes it untestable in the smoke suite and non-deterministic in production. Un-voiding (`SET voided_at = NULL`) does correctly abort. The predicate should key on the state, not the value: `WHEN OLD.voided_at IS NOT NULL`.

MINOR / CLAIM-VS-BEHAVIOUR: indexRationale asserts workout_log_sets_progress_idx is 'COVERING: the months-long progress graph and the player's PREVIOUS column read entirely from the index', and cites its own verification as 'SEARCH ... USING INDEX workout_log_sets_progress_idx'. Those two statements contradict each other -- SQLite reports 'USING COVERING INDEX' when an index actually covers. EXECUTED on the stated query (SELECT local_date, weight_kg, reps, e1rm_canonical_kg ... ORDER BY local_date DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50), the plan is `SEARCH workout_log_sets USING INDEX workout_log_sets_progress_idx (client_user_id=? AND exercise_id=?)` -- no COVERING, so every returned row still costs a table lookup. The important half of the claim does hold: no TEMP B-TREE, the DESC ordering is satisfied by the index. Everything else about the file is executable: the migration applies cleanly on top of 001-009 at user_version 10, integrity_check = ok, foreign_key_check = empty. WITHOUT ROWID on body_area_muscle_map (composite PK, no FTS5) is legal; STORED generated columns chaining (volume_kg and e1rm_canonical_kg both reference the generated effective_load_kg) is legal and computes correctly (100kg x 5 -> 500 volume, 116.6667 e1rm); partial indexes over generated columns build; `IS NOT (SELECT ...)` in trg_log_rollup_truthful parses and passes the recompute triggers with no float drift (12 imperial sets summed to 6123.4969949999995 and the truthful trigger accepted it, then accepted 5613.20557875 after a void on a CLOSED log); and `ALTER TABLE onboarding_profiles ADD COLUMN timezone TEXT CHECK (...)` is accepted -- a CHECK on an added column is not among SQLite's ALTER TABLE restrictions.
